focus.title: What I'm building toward
focus.lede: Where I'm deliberately taking my testing next. These are areas I'm studying and building projects in, not years of production experience.

items.title: Poker solver validation
items.text: Testing invariants, numerical tolerances, regressions, metamorphic properties and outputs where there may not be a perfect oracle.

items.title: AI and model quality
items.text: Evaluating whether outputs make sense, designing robust test datasets and understanding model-quality trade-offs.

items.title: Real-time poker systems
items.text: WebSockets, reconnects, idempotency, duplicate events, ordering, concurrency and state recovery.

items.title: Game integrity
items.text: Testing the data quality and systems used around botting, RTA, collusion and behavioral anomalies, knowing that a simple model can't conclusively prove cheating.

challenges.title: Hard problems I've tested
challenges.lede: Complex systems fail in combinations, state transitions and edge cases long before they fail in the happy path. These are examples of how I approach that kind of problem.

companies.context: Threat modeling SaaS. End-to-end automation with Playwright and TypeScript.

items.title: A rules engine with a combinatorial space
items.problem: A rule could depend on questionnaire answers, components, trust zones, data flows, security classifications or custom fields, and trigger several actions at once. Covering it by copying a flow per combination would have produced a huge, fragile suite.
approach: Page Objects and shared helpers for the complex screens
Entities created through the API when the UI added nothing to the test
Unique data per run, so runs never collide

items.title: Questionnaires that drive business rules
items.problem: An answer could show a question, insert another answer or produce a conclusion that fired a further rule. Each change had to be checked against the state before it, including what must not happen.
approach: Controlled starting states for every scenario
Setup kept apart from rule execution, so a failure points at its cause
Negative cases where a rule has to stay silent

items.title: Data that breaks where clean data doesn't
items.problem: UTF-8 text and double quotes in questions and answers could break saving or rule evaluation, and none of it showed up with tidy test data.
approach: Edge-case values in the suite on purpose
Round-trip checks from the UI through the API to storage and back

items.title: A flaky suite made reliable
items.problem: Elements existed in the DOM before they were ready, selectors matched more than one element, and positional selectors could pass on the wrong one.
approach: Semantic locators: getByRole, getByLabel and filters by context
Waits on observable state instead of fixed sleeps
Failures clear enough to tell a test problem from a product bug

items.title: Dynamic forms across UI, API and data
items.problem: Custom Fields and Security Content mixed dynamic forms, validations and references between entities, and backend errors surfaced in the UI.
approach: Checks on messages, state and persistence, not only on the click
Positive and negative cases for every constraint

items.title: Test architecture that scales
items.problem: Every new condition or action threatened to mean another copied flow.
approach: Page Objects, API helpers and data factories
Parameterized scenarios for variants that share setup and assertions
Reuse without hiding what each test checks

feature.title: How many CI containers a test suite needs
feature.text: End-to-end tests ran in 7 CI containers, one per product module. My first model balanced them and was 42% faster in a one-worker test run, but only about 8% with the 5 workers production used. Modelling the workers showed that 4 containers would be faster than 7 and cost 41% less.

link.sr: about how many CI containers a test suite needs

method.title: How I work
method.quote: I test software the way I was taught to do maths: state the problem precisely, argue every step, don't skip details.

steps.title: State the problem precisely
steps.text: Before I test or optimize anything, I write down what is given, the rules and the goal. That's how a slow CI pipeline became an optimization model.

link.label: See it in the CI case →

steps.title: Define what must be true first
steps.text: I agree on what has to hold for a feature to be done before a single test exists, in refinement and design reviews. A gap found in a ticket costs a comment; found in production, it costs a hotfix.

steps.title: Test at the layer where the defect can exist
steps.text: Rules and contracts get API tests; user flows get end-to-end tests. Running the same specs against a mock and the real API found a defect neither run could see alone.

steps.title: Use explicit test-design techniques
steps.text: Equivalence partitioning, boundary values, decision tables and state transitions, named in each test, so a reviewer can see what is covered and what isn't.

steps.title: Investigate until the root cause is clear
steps.text: A failing test is a question. I keep digging until I can say whether the product, the data, the environment or the test itself is wrong.

steps.title: Automate evidence, not just clicks
steps.text: A bug report should carry what a developer needs to reproduce it: console, network and the exact steps. I built a Chrome extension to capture it.

principle.label: Principle
principle.title: When there is no perfect oracle, test relationships and invariants.
principle.text: Quantitative and AI-driven systems don't always have one exact expected value. Then I test what must stay true: constraints, consistency between related inputs, metamorphic relationships, numerical tolerances and regressions against known outputs. It's how I test the core of CI Shard Advisor, and the whole point of my Solver Validation Lab.

poker.title: Poker is domain knowledge, not a hobby line on my CV
poker.text: I've played poker for roughly a decade, with significant time in Spin & Go formats, and I study with GTO Wizard. Concepts such as EV, equity, ranges, combinations, blockers, stack depth and strategic trade-offs are already part of how I reason, not terminology I learned for a job application.

career.title: Where I've worked
career.lede: Five years in QA, all of them automating tests.

jobs.context: Telecom OSS platform for EWE, a German telecom and energy provider, built on TM Forum standards
bullets: Design and run the tests for TM Forum service-order flows in Jira and Xray: add, modify, delete, suspend and reactivate.
Building API automation with Karate against TM Forum APIs.
Built a one-click Postman smoke suite that checks every service after a production deployment.

jobs.context: International cybersecurity SaaS for threat modeling, remote
bullets: Built a Python MILP model to split end-to-end tests across CI containers: 42% faster in a one-worker benchmark. Modelling the 5 production workers showed 4 containers instead of 7 would be about 8% faster and 41% cheaper.
Led the testing strategy for the Security Content module, a core part of the product, across backend, API and frontend.
Designed Playwright and TypeScript automation for a combinatorial rules engine, with Page Objects, API-backed setup and data factories.
Automated backend APIs in Java with REST Assured and JUnit 5: schema validation, negative cases and traceability.
Worked on the TestCafe to Playwright migration: about 80% less run time and a more stable suite.

jobs.context: Field service management SaaS, several client projects, remote
bullets: Moved client projects from mostly manual testing to automated end-to-end suites in Cypress.
Reported 500+ defects prioritized by product risk and business impact, and validated data with SQL.
Onboarded and mentored teammates on QA tooling and automation.
